One ongoing frustration is the lack of effort I see being put towards near-term, achievable crash projects to do good with AI at a national scale, whether those efforts are by the AI labs or by policymakers & NGOs. Some obvious ideas to explore suggested by the data we have so far: universal tutoring to support classroom learning, second opinions on healthcare, financial literacy/scam avoidance, and making government services easy to access. These are hard problems, and I know because over the past 20 years I have worked extensively on building tutoring and financial literacy programs, which were always limited by existing technology. Now, real gains are likely achievable with AI, which should be a big deal. Yes, you would want to do careful design and studies before rolling things out. And yes, those efforts might fail. But, if done right, national programs could lead to big gains in public good for seemingly intractable problems. And they don't require AIs beyond current models to pull off.
We should be more ambitious about trying to solve hard problems, rather than waiting for a nation of geniuses in a data center to solve them for us.

Brilliant paper on optimizing agent environments. This is an extremely important skill if you work with agents today. You can make a lot of improvements by optimizing the environments agents operate in. Many agents work inside a shared workspace, such as a company's Slack or a set of documents and tickets. EnvOpt changes what that workspace holds and how it is presented to the agent. A coding agent runs the target agent on training tasks without graders or reference answers, edits the environment, and stops based on a validation set. Haiku 4.5's pass rate also rises by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5 with 68.1% lower cost. On top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness, it lowers cost by another 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy. On AutomationBench, it cut Claude Haiku 4.5's cost by 72.7%. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07372 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/envopt-automated-optimization-for-agent-environments-2611.07372

Weight memory vs. retrieval in agents. Brilliant work from Amazon. This work shows weight memory can outperform text memory on recall of user facts. But the best part is that you can leverage both. Using the same model and user data, this work shows that plain fine-tuning stores user facts in weights at 36.9% accuracy, while on-policy self-distillation reaches 59.9%. That second number also beats retrieval. On eight HaluMem-Long users, the distilled model answers with no retrieved context and beats MemOS-style retrieval (47.8%), extracted context (51.9%), and the raw dialogue (51.3%). The gain holds for every user and at 4B, 9B, and 27B. How it works: a teacher, which is the same model reading the user's memory, trains a student that has to answer without it. Weight memory has clear limits. It forgets older facts and cannot tell when something was never recorded. A verify-then-regenerate router checks each answer against the text store and adds 6.2 points. The recommendation is to keep a text store for recent and missing facts, and move stable user knowledge into weights. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05636 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/route-to-remember-adaptive-memory-selection-for-llm-agents-2611.05636

Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses A training method that uses complementary sibling harnesses to rescue failed agent rollouts and transfers those behaviors into a single policy that still works under the original harness.

If you want to learn how to build self-improving harnesses, check out this paper. They present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for in-harness learning and adaptation during ongoing work. Harness optimization usually runs offline, so it needs a representative dataset and many expensive runs before the agent improves. Exo moves that loop into normal task execution. The agent edits its own harness code while it works. A small protected layer keeps the execution history and controls which policy version is active, so every change can be inspected. On AppWorld and SREGym, Exo cuts held-out model cost by 35 to 61% against the same starting policy without self-editing, with comparable correctness. Mean AppWorld task time drops 13%, and median SREGym diagnosis time drops 35%. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00463 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/exo-an-architecture-for-self-improving-systems-at-runtime-2611.00463

Banger report on foundation decision models. This work presents a 27B open decision model that lands within 1.6 points of Claude Opus 5.5 on Decision Bench v4 and answers in 183 ms instead of 3.5s. Nace AI released Drex, a family of four open decision models at 8B, 9B, 35B with 3B active, and 27B. You give the model a state, such as a document, a record, or an agent's context, plus questions with a fixed set of options. It returns a probability for each option without generating text. The 27B Max model scores 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4.1 suite, against 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0. On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with GPT-6 Sol and d3-turbo. It also has the best accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Model Training: After fine-tuning, training adds reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF). A teacher model proposes a probability for each option, and the verified answer adjusts it, so the model trains on calibrated targets in place of one-hot labels. RLAF adds 2.0 Decision Index points, and a consistency loss lowers the rate of flipped answers when the options are reordered from 6.3% to 4.2%.
